explanations.explanation: This feature fires on very short BPE fragments (single letters, 1–2-char pieces, digits or symbols) rather than full words—i.e. initials, acronyms, month/day abbreviations, equation or code tokens and other tiny subword or metadata markers.

Feature 1 (“…felt ‘intimidated’ by Jeff Bridges” etc.):  
This feature flags passages expressing a subject’s sense of being overwhelmed or daunted by a more experienced or eminent person (i.e. “intimidation” narratives).

Feature 2 (“Empowering Women to Embrace Their God-Given Design…,” “First moments One: A Poem,” “My body grows…”):  
This feature marks chapter- or section-level titles in inspirational/spiritual or pregnancy‐focused prose and poetry.

Feature 3 (“News,” “UPDATE: Tips…,” “Buck Danny,” “Cold Weekend,” product guides, blog posts, transcript headings, etc.):  
This feature detects document‐ or section‐level headings and headlines across diverse genres (news articles, blog entries, transcripts, product guides, etc.).

This feature is a general “sentence‐boundary” detector: it lights up on end-of-utterance markers (periods, question marks, exclamation points, closing brackets or quotes—even language-specific full‐stops), and more weakly on line-break or hyphenation points. In other words, it signals that the model is hitting the end of a sentence or clause.
This feature detects the opening “<?” token that kicks off a code‐or‐markup block (e.g. “<?php,” “<?xml …?>,” etc.), i.e. the file-level processing-instruction or script‐start marker.

This neuron fires on “index‐style” tokens used to label or enumerate items—e.g. standalone numbers (years, chapter or image indices, array or list positions, exponent digits, numeric constants) and similarly short boundary markers (like the “.c” file‐extension token). In other words, it picks out tokens whose primary role is to index or identify entries in text or code.

This neuron detects Title-Case headings and labels—i.e. the capitalized names, titles or section/menu headings (often followed by punctuation) that mark the start of an article, menu entry, code/license header, product name, etc.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is basically a “formatting/markup subtoken” detector.  It lights up on the little non-semantic pieces you see in structured text—single punctuation marks (dots, colons, parentheses), underscores in LaTeX subscripts, tiny subword chunks like chemical prefixes (“rham–”), taxonomic suffixes (“–les”), roman-numeral tokens (“II”), section markers and the like—i.e. the bits that signal formatting, metadata or domain-specific naming rather than carry ordinary lexical meaning.

This neuron is basically a “full-stop” detector in news/Wikipedia-style text. It lights up on the period token (and on isolated headline‐style tokens that effectively mark section or sentence boundaries), whether that period is ending a sentence, an abbreviation (“Sept.”), a decimal (“100.2”), or closing out a short title/heading line.

explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on the period that terminates a standalone boilerplate or heading line—e.g. the final “.” in copyright/license headers, disclaimers or titles in code comments and docs.

This neuron appears to fire whenever the model encounters a modifier that marks degree, status or classification—comparative/superlative words (more, less, high, second, largest, rising), past-participle adjectives describing a state or outcome (supervised, failed, delayed, enlarged, advanced, dilated, inflammatory), or stage-labels and similar descriptors (stage, global, end-stage)—across scientific, medical, legal and economic contexts.

This feature flags lexical markers of modality—words that signal potentiality, ability, likelihood or predisposition (e.g. “able,” “prone,” “going to,” “possibility,” “due,” “aware,” “hopes,” “willing,” “supposed”) across diverse contexts.
This neuron is a detector for the “.” token (the full‐stop/period), especially when used as an abbreviation marker or at the end of titles and sentences in Wikipedia-style text.

explanations.explanation:
1. Feature 1 (bold O in “Procedure CLR_TRIGGER_NAUDOJASI” block)  
   Recognizes Microsoft SQL Server error report headers (lines beginning with “Msg …, Level …, State …, Procedure …, Line …”).

2. Feature 2 (bold BE in `__MayaDM_POLICYCUBE_H__`)  
   Detects C++ header‐guard macros in the Maya Data Model code (the “…_H” pattern, here “POLICYCUBE_H”).

3. Feature 3 (bold DER in `__CPROVER_UT_SYMBOL_TABLE_BUILDER_H__`)  
   Marks C++ header‐guard macro segments in Diffblue’s symbol-table-builder headers (the “…BUILDER_H” suffix).

4. Feature 4 (bold O in `__LLVM_MC_SECTION_MACHO_H__`)  
   Flags C++ header‐guard macros in LLVM Mach-O section code (the “MC_SECTION_MACHO_H” pattern).

5. Feature 5 (bold CODE in `set(POLLY_IOS_13_4DEP…_BITCODE_CMAKE)`)  
   Identifies CMake configuration commands for enabling iOS bitcode in the Polly project.

6. Feature 6 (bold 0 in media/codec blocks)  
   Matches FFmpeg-style media‐stream metadata lines (stream indices, codec IDs, dimensions), especially numeric “0” tokens.

7. Feature 7 (bold INK in `THIRD_PARTY_BLINK_RENDERER_…_H`)  
   Picks out C++ header‐guard macros in Chromium’s Blink renderer code (the “BLINK_RENDERER…_H” pattern).

8. Feature 8 (bold EXEC in `EXECS = …`)  
   Detects Makefile variable assignments listing executables (the “EXECS =” idiom).

9. Feature 9 (bold ER in `LIBANGLE_RENDERER_VULKAN_CACHE_UTILS_H`)  
   Captures C++ header‐guard macros in the ANGLE project’s Vulkan cache utilities (“…RENDERER…_H”).

10. Feature 10 (bold OUTPUT in `IGLOO_DEFAULTTESTRESULTSOUTPUT_H`)  
    Recognizes C++ header‐guard macros in the IGLOO testing framework (“…OUTPUT_H”).

11. Feature 11 (bold KS in `L1MUDTTFMASKS_H`)  
    Flags C++ header‐guard macros in DTT task definitions (“…MASKS_H”).

12. Feature 12 (bold PET in `COMPONENTS_NTP_SNIPPETS_STATUS_H`)  
    Identifies C++ header‐guard macros in Chromium’s NTP-snippets component (“…SNIPPETS…_H”).

13. Feature 13 (bold GE in `QHULLRIDGE_H`)  
    Marks C++ header‐guard macros in Qhull geometry code (“…RIDGE_H”).

14. Feature 14 (bold ER in `_IP6T_OWNER_H`)  
    Captures C header‐guard macros in Linux-kernel user‐space headers (“IP6T_OWNER_H”).

15. Feature 15 (bold ER in `V8_CCTEST_COMPILER_CODEGEN_TESTER_H`)  
    Detects C++ header‐guard macros in the V8 engine’s codegen tester (“…CODEGEN_TESTER_H”).

16. Feature 16 (bold ients in “/var/www/clients/…”)  
    Recognizes PHP session-start warning messages and file‐path patterns under “/var/www/clients/…”, highlighting “clients.”

This neuron is simply flagging the start of a new word‐or‐subword unit (e.g. the initial letter(s) of a word—capital or lowercase—or leading apostrophe in a contraction), regardless of language or genre.

This neuron seems to fire on the “inner” piece of any small, rigidly delimited sequence—e.g. the middle number of a DOI or citation key (54, 647, 777, 40, 73), the central term in an institutional title (National in Oak Ridge National Laboratory), or the key exclusion word in boilerplate lists (without). In other words, it marks the core component of structured multi-part identifiers or legal/administrative clauses.

This feature fires on “boilerplate” at the top of a file or document – things like she-bang lines (#!/usr/bin/env …), PHP’s <?php tag, JS/Perl “use strict” pragmas, initial import/require statements or metadata comments, even the first sentence period in a news article. In other words, it marks the start-of-file/section boilerplate or opening directive.

This neuron seems to be a “chunk-boundary” detector: it fires on the last meaningful token of a content chunk just before a small, highly predictable unit—whether that be a function word (“as _long_ as,” “as _far_ as,” “Posted _by_”), punctuation (“7_:_00 pm”), or the next segment of a compound identifier or name (the “DA” in WebDAV, “ST” in CROSSTOOL, “Late” in LaTeX, “ant” in Qantas, “ven” in Provenzano, “ic” in “.icn,” “A” in a GUID, etc.). In other words, it marks the hinge between a content word and the tiny grammatical or morphological piece that follows.

This feature fires on the structured “header” lines of legal and other formal documents—tokens marking case captions, court names, docket numbers, publication status, dates, and similar metadata in document headers.

This feature fires on the invisible “hinges” between one block of prose and the next—e.g. the end of a headline or paragraph and the start of a byline, caption, quotation header, list header, sub-heading or other metadata—marking structural breaks in an article or post.

This feature fires on those “boilerplate” lines that sit at the top (or head) of a document or code unit—copyright/license comments, include/import/package/namespace directives, XML/HTML or script tags, SQL “CREATE FUNCTION” headers, Python `from __future__` imports, YouTube “Watch” headers, etc.—i.e. file- or section-level metadata/declaration tokens.

The feature is a detector for high-level discourse cues—words like what, so, basically, obviously, like, finally, in light of, beyond, etc.—that speakers use to signpost explanations, emphasis or transitions in running text.

This feature fires on the “.” token when it’s being used as the end‐of‐abbreviation or citation marker in highly structured text (e.g. after an author’s middle initial “M.”, the “No.” in docket numbers, court reporter abbreviations like “F.” in “417 F.2d 1112,” taxonomic abbreviations “subsp.,” version numbers “1.0,” etc.).

explanations.explanation: This feature lights up on “noise” tokens that aren’t real words—either the Unicode replacement character (�) that shows up when text or markup is garbled, or the short opaque alphanumeric strings you see in URLs (e.g. Twitter’s t.co codes or tweet IDs). It’s essentially a “non‐linguistic/token-garbage” detector.

This feature fires on English auxiliary (helping) verbs—especially “do/does/did” plus the modals “can/could,” “will/would,” etc.—marking the grammatical signals used for questions, negation, and modality across diverse contexts.

This neuron is essentially a “statement/sentence-end” detector in formal, highly structured text.  It peaks on the final punctuation or newline that closes off a top-level declaration—e.g. the end of a Python import line or the period ending the standard “The present invention relates to…” sentence in patent prose.

explanations.explanation: This feature detects sentence-initial discourse markers—typically a preposition or infinitival verb (e.g. “Following,” “To,” “For,” “After,” “Experimental,” “We”)—that frame the new sentence in temporal, causal or purposive context.

This neuron fires on little “annotation” markers that introduce metadata or declarations across genres—things like the `@` in “(@user…)” at‐mentions, the `:` in Go struct tags (e.g. ``json:"foo"``), the `type`/`interface` keyword or function name in code definitions, leading `#` in license/comments, even the `{` in a LaTeX command. In short, it lights up on the punctuation or keywords that kick off a structured annotation or definition block.

This neuron is picking out the period “.” when it’s acting as a delimiter—whether ending a sentence, marking an abbreviation (e.g. “M.D.”, “D.C.”), or separating file extensions and code tokens (e.g. “.tif”, “.sh”, “.h”).

This feature fires on tokens that mark the *start* of a special, multi‐character unit—be it a gene/protein name or acronym (e.g. TSPAN2, CETP, SPLV), a domain‐specific term (cardiac, immunogenic), a code‐level identifier or operator boundary (.TOGGLE, +), or an XML/HTML tag bracket (</Value>).  In other words, it detects the boundary/prefix of key domain‐specific entities and constructs across text, code, math, and markup.
